content.title: Apollo 17 astronaut moon landing last manned lunar mission: Pictures
content.text: AP/NASA PHOTO Dec 19, 2019, 5:27 PM UTC Humans haven't set foot on the moon in nearly half a century, but photos from the small number of trips remain source of fascination. People first landed on the moon in 1969 as part of the Apollo 11 mission, one of only six total manned lunar missions. Apollo 17 was the last, three years after the first, and it landed safely back on earth 47 years ago today. Now, President Trump says he plans to send astronauts back to the moon as soon as 2024, but concerns over money and NASA's culture might make that timeline overly ambitious, according to some astronauts. These photos show the last time humans were on the moon. Ronald Evans, pictured here with his wife Jan Pollom, was Command Module Pilot for the Apollo 17 Lunar Landing Mission, which took off from Cape Kennedy in Florida on December 7. AP Photo/NASA Dr. Schmitt was the lunar module pilot. AP photo/Jim Kerlin Harrison Schmitt, Ronald Evans, and Eugene Cernan prepared to go into space. Bettmann / Contributor The command module orbited the moon. Corbis/Corbis via Getty Images Once on the moon, astronauts collected lunar samples... AP/NASA PHOTO ...like this 3.5 billion year old rock, sometimes called "The Goodwill Sample." Samples from it were gifted to every country on earth. AP Photo The Evans family watched two of the astronauts explore the moon on TV, while Ronald Evans orbited the moon in the command module. AP Photo Cernan drove the Lunar Roving Vehicle around the landing site. Astronaut Eugene A. Cernan takes the lunar roving vehicle out for a spin during the Apollo 17 mission, December 12, 1972. NASA The astronauts took a photo of earth from the spacecraft. AP photo/NASA According to NASA, astronauts spent 75 hours on the moon's surface during the mission. AP/NASA PHOTO The Evans family and others waited for news of a safe landing. AP Photo/NASA The command module landed back on earth in the Pacific Ocean on December 19, 1972. AP Photo/PL The family and supporters cheered as they watched the landing on TV. AP Photo/NASA On December 21, Evans was reunited with his wife and two children in Houston.
